opus-5.5.text:
I think there are a few layers to it. At the most basic level, NVIDIA is a platform company. Our job is to make the whole ecosystem move faster, and AI moves fastest when people can build on each other's work. When we release open models, like our Cosmos world foundation models for physical AI, the goal isn't to compete with our customers. It's to give developers, researchers, and startups a strong starting point so they don't have to train everything from scratch.

Physical AI is a good example. If you want to build a robot or an autonomous vehicle, you need a model that understands how the physical world works: how objects move, how light behaves, what happens when something gets pushed. Training that kind of model takes an enormous amount of data and compute, and very few organizations can afford it. If every robotics company had to do that alone, the field would move very slowly. So we pretrain these foundation models, open them up, and let people post-train them on their own data for their own use cases. That lowers the barrier a lot.

The second layer is that building these models makes us better at what we do. When we train large models ourselves, we run into the same problems our customers do: data pipelines, tokenizers, training efficiency, inference. That pushes us to improve our hardware, software stack, and tools. In a sense, we're our own first customer.

The third layer is trust and transparency. With open weights, and in many cases open data curation pipelines and recipes, people can see how the model was built, evaluate it, find its weaknesses, and improve on it. That's very healthy for the research community, and especially important in physical AI, where safety really matters.

So in short, it's about accelerating the ecosystem. If the whole field grows, more people build AI applications, and that's good for everyone, including NVIDIA.

r001.rationale: It says open models give developers, researchers, and startups a strong starting point to build for their own use cases, lowering the barrier for them to pursue their ideas.

r002.rationale: It describes accelerating the ecosystem but does not say that more diverse ideas give users more choices.

r003.rationale: It says ecosystem growth benefits everyone, including NVIDIA, but does not present realizing diverse ideas as a driver of social progress.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. That's a question I think about a lot, because at first glance it may seem counterintuitive. NVIDIA is a company that sells hardware, so why spend so much effort building models and then giving them away?

The simplest answer is that we are a platform company. Our success depends on the entire ecosystem succeeding. When developers, startups, researchers, and enterprises can take a strong model and build on top of it, the whole field moves faster, and ultimately more useful applications get built. Those applications run on compute. So open models are not charity for us. They are how we grow the pie rather than fight over a slice of it.

The second reason is more specific to the areas I work on, which are physical AI and world models with Cosmos. In robotics and autonomous systems, the number of people who can train a foundation model from scratch is very small. The data is hard to collect, the compute cost is enormous, and most robotics companies simply cannot afford it. If we keep those models closed, we are essentially telling the robotics community to wait. If we open them, a small team can fine-tune on their own robot, their own factory, their own driving data, and get to something useful in weeks instead of years. I genuinely believe physical AI will not take off unless the foundation layer is accessible.

There is also a research motivation. I came from the research side, and I still see myself as a researcher. Progress in this field has always come from people being able to inspect, reproduce, and improve on each other's work. When we release not only weights but also the data pipelines, the training recipes, and the evaluation tools, we invite the community to find the problems we missed and push the frontier in directions we would never have thought of. That feedback loop makes our next model better as well.

And finally, I think there is a question of trust and choice. Many enterprises, especially in manufacturing, healthcare, or anything safety critical, do not want to send their data to an API they cannot control. They want to run the model themselves, modify it, and understand it. Open models give them that option. It means AI is not controlled by just two or three companies, and I think that is healthy for everyone, including us.

So when people ask me about the purpose, I would say it is this: we want to be the company that builds the tools that let everyone else build. Open models are the most direct expression of that.

r001.rationale: It says developers, startups, researchers, and enterprises can build on strong models, fine-tune them for their own needs, and build useful applications.

r002.rationale: The response mentions choice and letting enterprises run models themselves, but does not connect a greater diversity of ideas reaching users to giving users more choices.

r003.rationale: It says open models help the field move faster and enable useful applications, but does not present realizing diverse ideas as a driver of social progress.

astra-6.text:
I think the purpose is to help more people build with AI. Training a strong foundation model requires a lot of compute, data, and expertise. When you make models openly available, developers can start from that foundation and adapt it to their own applications, rather than having to build everything from scratch.

For NVIDIA, that also helps grow the ecosystem. As more people experiment with models and turn them into useful products, there is more demand for the computing infrastructure that supports them. So there’s a business motivation, but it aligns with making AI more accessible and helping innovation happen faster.

r001.rationale: The response says developers can adapt openly available models for applications, but it does not specify ambitious people outside major AI companies or frame the models as enabling them to realize their own ideas.

r002.rationale: It discusses broader experimentation and useful products, but does not say that greater diversity of ideas gives users more choices.

r003.rationale: It says open models can help innovation happen faster, but does not present diverse ideas as a driver of social progress.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the purpose is to enable more people to build with AI. When you release a model openly, developers and researchers can experiment with it, adapt it to their own problems, and build on what you’ve done. That also creates a feedback loop: you learn what works, where the limitations are, and what people actually need.

For NVIDIA, that connects to the broader goal of making AI useful. A model by itself is only one piece. People need tools and infrastructure to turn it into an application. Open models help that whole ecosystem grow.

r001.rationale: The response says open models let more people build and adapt AI, but it does not specify ambitious people outside major AI companies or frame this as a chance to realize their own ideas.

r002.rationale: It mentions experimentation and adaptation, but does not say that bringing diverse ideas to users gives users more choices.

r003.rationale: The response discusses growing the AI ecosystem and making AI useful, but does not present diverse ideas as a driver of social progress.
